domain: Historical Anthropology / Material Culture / Evolutionary Linguistics
topic_summary: Analysis of the historical shift from edge-to-edge bite configuration to overbite/overjet preservation in human populations, driven by adoption of knife-and-fork eating technology circa 1700s-1800s. The shift enabled labiodental phoneme innovation (f/v sounds) and represents a case of anatomical drift through tool-mediated behavioral change with no deliberate architect.

key_entities: Fork-and-knife eating technology (material culture innovation, Europe 1600s-1800s)
Edge-to-edge bite configuration (ancestral human/ape dental occlusion pattern)
Overbite/overjet configuration (adolescent dental pattern preserved into adulthood)
Labiodental phonemes (f/v sounds, post-Neolithic linguistic innovation)
key_tensions: Biological constraint (ancestral bite pattern) vs cultural practice (cutlery-mediated food processing)
key_mechanisms: Mechanical feedback loop: fork pre-cuts food → reduced masticatory force → adolescent overbite persists into adulthood
Phonetic enablement: overbite configuration makes labiodental sounds (f/v) articulatorily easier → linguistic drift
key_absences: No institutional authority enforcing bite configuration change
No identifiable beneficiary class from the anatomical shift
No deliberate selection pressure or eugenic program
